indicatorNotes.tumbles: A tumble sends whatever falls end over end, so the letters beside it land in a different order.

blocks.note: anagram fodder, twelve letters
anagram indicator

annotation.surface: A roofer loses his footing up on the tiles and comes down with everything else.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Slip' and 'tumbles' both mean falling, so the pair reads as one accident rather than as fodder plus instruction. Counting twelve letters against the enumeration settles it.
annotation.definitionFit: A professor is a scholar by trade, so professorial carries the learned, bookish sense that scholarly describes.

entries.clue: Goad party on the rise under electoral system (4)

indicatorNotes.on the rise: Something on the rise is climbing, and in a down entry a climbing word is read from the bottom up.
indicatorNotes.under: Under puts the party beneath the electoral system in this column, so the system's letters are written first.

blocks.note: PR is proportional representation, the voting system Britain argues about
a party is a do, climbing the column

annotation.surface: A political party's fortunes climbing under a new way of counting votes.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Party' in a clue full of elections is the social kind, a do. Proportional representation is the system where seats are shared out in step with votes cast.
annotation.definitionFit: A prod is a sharp poke given to get someone moving, which is what a goad does, and both work as noun or verb.

entries.clue: Near the coast connected to prop (7)

blocks.note: a switch that is connected is on
to shore a wall up is to prop it

annotation.surface: A cable running near the coast is wired up to a supporting post.
annotation.walkthrough: There is no anagram or hidden run to spot here, just two everyday words stacked. 'Prop' looks like a noun and has to be heard as a verb before anything moves.
annotation.definitionFit: Onshore means situated on the land at the water's edge - onshore drilling, an onshore wind farm - which is what near the coast describes.

indicatorNotes.away: Taking a thing away is removing it altogether, so the letter named next to it drops out.

blocks.note: to remove a pencil mark is to erase it
r is the standard abbreviation for right, as on a map or a glove

annotation.surface: Someone soothes the situation and clears the mess up immediately.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Right away' reads as 'immediately' and is really two instructions: a letter, and an order to lose it. The R that goes is the one at the front of the longer verb.
annotation.definitionFit: To ease a pain or a burden is to relieve it, and both verbs take the same objects and the same third-person -s.

entries.clue: Walked with authority in Dorset, possibly (6)

indicatorNotes.possibly: Possibly says the letters given are only one of the ways they might be arranged, so another is wanted.

blocks.note: anagram fodder, six letters
anagram indicator

annotation.surface: Somebody marching about purposefully, somewhere in the West Country.
annotation.walkthrough: Dorset is a county on England's south coast, and 'possibly' beside a place name reads as vagueness about where the walking happened. The whole county is the fodder.
annotation.definitionFit: Strode is the past tense of stride, and a stride is the long confident step of someone who is in charge.

blocks.note: re means concerning, the word at the head of a memo
verse is poetry

annotation.surface: A memo about poetry that ends by telling the reader to back up.
annotation.walkthrough: RE for 'regarding' is the most reliable two letters in cryptics, and it hides best at the start of a clue where it looks like ordinary preamble. The comma is the only join.
annotation.definitionFit: To reverse is to move backwards, as a car reverses out of a drive, so verb and phrase swap straight over.

entries.clue: Speak off the cuff in Maidenhead library (2-3)

indicatorNotes.in: In says the word is sitting inside the words that follow, rather than being described by what they mean.

blocks.note: the run crosses the gap: the end of MaidenheAD and the start of LIBrary

annotation.surface: Someone talking without notes in a library in a Berkshire town.
annotation.walkthrough: Maidenhead is a town on the Thames west of London, picked because its tail and the head of 'library' meet exactly where the hyphen falls. Hidden runs that straddle a word break are the hardest to see.
annotation.definitionFit: To ad-lib is to improvise words on the spot with no script, which is what speaking off the cuff means.

indicatorNotes.containing: What contains something holds it inside, so the shorter word goes within the longer instead of beside it.
indicatorNotes.torn: A torn thing has come apart, and the pieces can be put back together in another order.

blocks.note: a memo is the office note, and it opens up to take the insertion
the three letters of NET, torn and reset

annotation.surface: A treasured note kept wrapped around a scrap of ripped netting.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Note' has three standard cryptic readings - memo, banknote, musical letter - and only the memo is long enough to swallow three more letters. 'Torn net' looks like flotsam rather than an instruction.
annotation.definitionFit: A memento is an object kept because it calls a person or an occasion to mind, which is what a souvenir is.

entries.clue: Ring a relative found at desert haven (5)

blocks.note: a ring is drawn as the letter O
the clue's own a, taken at face value
sis is the familiar short form of sister

annotation.surface: Phone a relative who has turned up at a watering hole in the desert.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface asks you to ring somebody up; the wordplay wants the shape of a ring. Short clues shrink their relatives - sis, bro, ma, pa - and 'relative' is the usual warning.
annotation.definitionFit: An oasis is the watered, fertile patch in a desert where travellers can stop safely, a haven in the plainest sense.

blocks.note: r is a run on a cricket scorecard
to evolve is to develop by degrees

annotation.surface: An instruction to turn, take to your heels and then grow into something better.
annotation.walkthrough: R for run comes off the cricket scorecard, where runs are tallied by the letter, and it is one of the commonest single letters in British cryptics. 'Turn and run' reads as one phrase and splits in two.
annotation.definitionFit: A wheel that revolves turns on its axis, so turn is the plain verb sense and swaps in directly.

entries.clue: Fairly big bar code lines revised (12)

indicatorNotes.revised: A revised text has been gone over and changed, and what changes here is the order the letters stand in.

blocks.note: anagram fodder, twelve letters
anagram indicator

annotation.surface: The stripes on a product's barcode have been redrawn since last time.
annotation.walkthrough: A barcode's lines genuinely do get revised when a product changes, which keeps the fodder reading as plain description. 'Fairly big' sounds too vague to be a definition until you hear it as 'a considerable amount'.
annotation.definitionFit: Considerable means large enough to be worth reckoning with, a considerable sum, which is the unmeasured largeness that fairly big points at.

indicatorNotes.made false: Making something false alters it from how it should stand, so the letters are set down wrongly on purpose.

blocks.note: anagram fodder, seven letters
anagram indicator

annotation.surface: A mouth capable of making a lie sound like the honest truth.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Mouth' is the river kind, where fresh water widens into the sea, not the one doing the talking. 'Say' looks like the usual 'for example' tag and is fodder instead.
annotation.definitionFit: An estuary is the tidal mouth of a river, and mouth is the standard geographical word for where a river ends.

entries.clue: Look now and then to find children's apparatus (3-3)

blocks.note: looking in the present tense
the same verb in the past: what you did then, not now

annotation.surface: Keep an eye out from time to time and you will come across the playground kit.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Now and then' reads as 'occasionally' and is really a pair of clocks, one set to the present and one to the past. The hyphenated enumeration confirms two halves of three.
annotation.definitionFit: A see-saw is the plank pivoted across a bar that children ride up and down, standard equipment in any playground.

indicatorNotes.storm: A storm throws about everything it hits, leaving the pieces lying in an order nobody chose.

blocks.note: anagram fodder, seven letters
anagram indicator

annotation.surface: Damage reported at a stretch of cliff once the bad weather has passed.
annotation.walkthrough: Coastal erosion makes the surface read like a news item, which hides seven letters sitting in the open. 'Trouble' is the transitive verb, not a noun for the damage.
annotation.definitionFit: To afflict someone is to trouble them with pain or distress, and trouble takes the same objects: illness afflicts, illness troubles.

blocks.note: the verb for rummaging nose-down through a drawer until something turns up
the animal itself, a weasel-family hunter worked down rabbit burrows

annotation.surface: Somebody hunting through the undergrowth for an escaped polecat.
annotation.walkthrough: 'For' is the hinge, and it makes the two halves read as one hunt. The verb came from the animal, which is why a ferreting search is a burrowing, nose-down one.
annotation.definitionFit: To ferret is to rummage and search about, and the ferret is the domesticated form of the polecat, tame enough to be worked down a rabbit hole.

blocks.note: re means about, the word at the head of a memo
a lease is the contract a tenant signs

annotation.surface: A statement given to the papers concerning somebody's rental contract.
annotation.walkthrough: In a newsroom a release is the prepared statement an organisation puts out, so the definition runs to two words and reads as part of the story. 'About' is the tiny word doing the work.
annotation.definitionFit: A press release is the statement an organisation issues to journalists, and in the trade it is shortened to its second word.

blocks.note: to rib somebody is to tease them
the eye of a needle is the small hole the thread goes through

annotation.surface: Someone joking about the tiny hole they have found in their dinner.
annotation.walkthrough: Ribbing is teasing and an eye is a needle's hole, so neither half comes from the butcher. The cut takes its name from the rib it is carved beside, which makes the first word look almost honest.
annotation.definitionFit: A rib-eye is the boneless steak cut from the middle of the rib section, a standard item on any menu.

entries.clue: However dye runs, rifle is easy to operate (4-8)

indicatorNotes.However: However means in whatever manner, so the letters may be set down in any arrangement at all.

blocks.note: anagram fodder, twelve letters
anagram indicator

annotation.surface: No matter how far the dye bleeds into it, the gun is still simple to handle.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Runs' is the word begging to be the signal, since dye that runs has spread everywhere, but it is fodder and the instruction is the 'However' standing at the front of the clue.
annotation.definitionFit: A user-friendly device is built so that an ordinary person can work it without the manual, which is being easy to operate.

indicatorNotes.mostly: Mostly asks for most of a word and not the whole of it, which means dropping its final letter.
indicatorNotes.in disguise: Anything in disguise is not showing its true shape, so the letters turn up rearranged.

blocks.note: UNSEEN handed over without its last letter
anagram indicator

annotation.surface: A tail who keeps out of sight and goes about it in costume.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Unseen' has to be trimmed before it is shuffled, and 'mostly' is the only word saying so. Following unseen and in disguise is exactly what a tail does, which is why the surface holds together.
annotation.definitionFit: To ensue is to follow on or come next, as in a scuffle ensued, so follow is the plain verb sense.

blocks.note: British slang for stealing, the same way pinch is
the shallow notches left in a surface, or in a chin after shaving

annotation.surface: A report of somebody making off with a few small joints of meat.
annotation.walkthrough: Both halves are everyday British: nicking is what a thief does, and a nick is what the razor leaves. The plural -s carries through both senses without changing anything.
annotation.definitionFit: To nick is to steal, which is what pinches means in the same slang register, and a nick is a small shallow cut.

blocks.note: the heraldic emblems a family is entitled to bear on a shield
the military sense, the guns and blades a country takes up in war

annotation.surface: A family crest hanging on the wall above a collection of old weapons.
annotation.walkthrough: Coats of arms began as the devices painted on a knight's shield, so the heraldic sense and the weapon sense grew from the same root. 'Displays' is the hinge and contributes no letters.
annotation.definitionFit: A family's arms are the heraldic emblems it bears, and arms in the older sense are the weapons those emblems were painted on.

entries.clue: I pester madly to get a welcome break (7)

indicatorNotes.madly: Doing a thing madly is doing it without order, so the letters come out in no sensible arrangement.

blocks.note: anagram fodder, seven letters
anagram indicator

annotation.surface: A nuisance admits to nagging without let-up in the hope of being given time off.
annotation.walkthrough: The 'I' is fodder rather than a character, a habit worth expecting whenever a clue speaks in the first person. 'Welcome' is part of the definition, not decoration.
annotation.definitionFit: A respite is a short interval of relief from something wearing, so it is a break and a welcome one by definition.

entries.clue: Maybe rocker is starting to compose musical (5)

indicatorNotes.starting to: Starting to points at the opening of the word that follows, so only its first letter is taken.

blocks.note: the first letter of compose and nothing more
Hair is the 1967 rock musical

annotation.surface: A rock musician sitting down to write the opening of a stage show.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Rocker' in the surface is a leather-jacketed musician, and the answer wants the rocking sort you sit in. Hair opened in 1967 and is the musical setters reach for when four letters are needed.
annotation.definitionFit: A rocking chair is one kind of chair, and 'maybe' warns that the clue names only an example of the answer.

entries.clue: Lessen stress over inability to stay still (12)

indicatorNotes.over: To knock a thing over is to upset it, and what has been upset no longer lies in the order it was in.

blocks.note: anagram fodder, twelve letters
anagram indicator

annotation.surface: Advice on cutting down the pressure somebody has been living under.
annotation.walkthrough: Fodder and answer are cousins in meaning, since lessening stress is the cure for what the answer names, and that is why the letters read as sense rather than as raw material.
annotation.definitionFit: Restlessness is the state of being unable to settle or keep still, in body or in mind, which the phrase spells out.
